title: Demonstrate an understanding of the use of different number bases and measurement units and an awareness of error in the context of relevant calculations

lessons.title: Number bases
lessons.html:
Our number system: base 10

We normally count in base 10 (decimal). It uses ten digits, 0 to 9, and each place is worth ten times the place to its right: units, tens, hundreds, thousands. For example, 2 345 means 2 thousands + 3 hundreds + 4 tens + 5 units.

Other bases you meet at work

Base 2 (binary) uses only 0 and 1. Computers, scales, PLC-controlled graders and electronic thermometers store numbers in binary. Each place is worth twice the place to its right: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and so on.

BinaryCalculationDecimal
1014 + 0 + 15
11008 + 4 + 0 + 012
1111116 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 131

To convert decimal to binary, divide repeatedly by 2 and write the remainders from bottom to top. Example: 13 ÷ 2 = 6 remainder 1; 6 ÷ 2 = 3 r 0; 3 ÷ 2 = 1 r 1; 1 ÷ 2 = 0 r 1. Reading upward: 1101.

Time: base 60

Time uses base 60 for minutes and seconds. 60 seconds = 1 minute; 60 minutes = 1 hour. This affects calculations: 1.5 hours is 1 hour 30 minutes, not 1 hour 50 minutes. To convert minutes to decimal hours, divide by 60: 45 minutes = 0.75 hours. This matters when calculating hours worked for wages.

Example: a shift runs from 06:45 to 15:15. From 06:45 to 14:45 is 8 hours, plus 30 minutes = 8 hours 30 minutes = 8.5 hours.

Counting in dozens and other groups

Some products are counted in groups, such as eggs in dozens (12) or trays of 30, or fruit in count sizes per carton. A tray system is like a base: 75 eggs = 2 trays of 30 + 15 eggs.

lessons.title: Measurement units and conversions
lessons.html:
The metric system (SI)

South Africa uses the metric system. Its prefixes are based on powers of 10, which makes conversion easy.

PrefixMeaningExamples
kilo (k)× 1 0001 km = 1 000 m; 1 kg = 1 000 g
centi (c)÷ 1001 m = 100 cm
milli (m)÷ 1 0001 L = 1 000 mL; 1 m = 1 000 mm

Common conversions

  • Mass: 1 ton (t) = 1 000 kg; 1 kg = 1 000 g.
  • Volume: 1 L = 1 000 mL; 1 m³ = 1 000 L.
  • Area: 1 hectare (ha) = 10 000 m².
  • Temperature: degrees Celsius (°C) is used in cold chain records.

Converting units

To convert from a big unit to a small unit, multiply. To convert from a small unit to a big unit, divide.

  • 2.4 t of fruit = 2.4 × 1 000 = 2 400 kg.
  • 750 g = 750 ÷ 1 000 = 0.75 kg.
  • A sanitiser dose of 5 mL per litre in a 200 L tank needs 5 × 200 = 1 000 mL = 1 L of concentrate. Always use the dose stated on the product label.

Rates and compound units

Many workplace measures combine units: kg/h for packing rate, L/ha for spray volume, km/h for speed, R/kg for price. Check that both parts are in matching units before calculating. Example: a line packs 1 200 kg in 40 minutes. Rate = 1 200 ÷ 40 = 30 kg per minute = 30 × 60 = 1 800 kg/h.

Imperial units

Some older equipment and imported machines use imperial units such as inches, pounds or PSI. Use conversion tables or the equipment manual: for example, 1 inch is about 25.4 mm and 1 pound is about 0.454 kg.

lessons.title: Accuracy, rounding and error
lessons.html:
No measurement is perfect

Every measurement has some error. Understanding error helps you decide if a result is good enough and avoid costly mistakes, such as underweight cartons or wrong chemical doses.

Sources of error

  • Instrument error: a scale that is not calibrated, a worn tape measure, a thermometer that reads high.
  • Reading error: reading a scale at an angle (parallax), misreading the decimal point.
  • Method error: weighing a carton without taring the scale, measuring temperature at the surface instead of the core.
  • Recording error: writing 1.8 instead of 18, or swapping digits.
  • Rounding error: rounding too early in a calculation.

Precision and tolerance

The precision of an instrument is the smallest unit it shows: a kitchen scale may show 1 g, a platform scale 0.5 kg. Specifications often allow a tolerance, a permitted range. A 10 kg carton specification might allow a range set by the customer; anything outside it is non-conforming.

Rounding

Round to a sensible number of places for the purpose: money to two decimal places (cents), carton mass to the scale's precision. Round only at the end of a calculation. If the digit after the rounding place is 5 or more, round up; otherwise round down. 12.346 kg rounded to one decimal = 12.3 kg; 12.36 kg = 12.4 kg.

Absolute and percentage error

If a check weight of 10.00 kg reads 10.15 kg on a scale, the absolute error is 0.15 kg. Percentage error = 0.15 ÷ 10 × 100 = 1.5%. If this exceeds the allowed limit, the scale must be recalibrated or taken out of use and reported.

Estimating to check

Estimate before calculating to catch big errors. If 48 cartons of 12.5 kg should weigh about 50 × 12.5 = 625 kg, a calculated answer of 6 000 kg is clearly wrong.

Key points

  • Base 10 is everyday counting; base 2 is used by computers; time uses base 60.
  • 1.5 hours is 1 hour 30 minutes; divide minutes by 60 for decimal hours.
  • Multiply to convert to smaller units, divide to convert to bigger units.
  • Errors come from instruments, reading, method, recording and rounding.
  • Round only at the end and check results with estimates.
  • Percentage error = error ÷ true value × 100.
